Check figures, postings, and documents for correct entry, mathematical accuracy, and proper codes (importance 92, Core) - highest-scored task found in this research; it is the timesheet, invoice and job-cost coding workload of B2B service back offices.
Reconcile or note and report discrepancies found in records (importance 82, Core) - matching client purchase orders, invoices and payments.
Develop sales presentations or proposals to explain service specifications (importance 81, Core) - RFP/proposal writing for consultancies, agencies and commercial cleaning bids.

Notify managers concerning the need for major repairs or additions to building operating systems (importance 80, Core) and requisition supplies or equipment (69, Core). automation_evidence.finding: Staggered rollout of a generative-AI chat assistant to 5,172 customer-support agents raised issues resolved per hour by 15% on average, with much larger gains for less-experienced workers (novice/low-skill gains around 34% in earlier drafts). Published, peer-reviewed version of the widely cited Fortune 500 software-firm study - the closest measured analogue to B2B service desks and staffing client-service teams.

Preregistered experiment with 453 college-educated professionals on occupation-specific mid-level writing tasks (managers, HR professionals, marketers, consultants): ChatGPT access cut average completion time by 40% and raised output quality by 18%. Preprint-adjacent caveat: tasks were 20-30 minute simulated writing, not live client work.

Field experiment with 758 BCG consultants: on 18 realistic consulting tasks judged inside AI capability, GPT-4 access produced 12.2% more tasks completed, 25.1% faster, at higher quality. On one task deliberately outside the frontier, AI users were significantly more likely to get the answer wrong - the 'jagged frontier' evidence for knowledge-intensive consultancies.

Randomised evaluation of an AI sourcing chatbot deployed by the French public employment service (late 2024) to caseworkers who support employers' hiring: probability of filling posted jobs rose 10-15%. Authors attribute the gain to freed caseworker time being reallocated to screening applications - the most direct labour-market-intermediary evidence found. Working paper (seminar version, 2026), not yet journal-published.

ACEC Research Institute report on AI in engineering (2025; 19 executive interviews, ACEC sentiment survey of 644 firm leaders, plus BST Global's global AEC survey): 68% of firms estimate AI could automate up to 29% of current tasks; AI use is most common in marketing and sales (81%) versus design and project delivery (36%), with AI-assisted proposal development named as a common application; 74% expect to hold staffing levels while increasing output. Self-reported estimates, not measured time savings.

Bullhorn GRID 2025 survey of 1,500+ recruitment professionals: recruiters spend an average 14.6 hours a week searching for candidates; autonomous search/match plus AI screening could return roughly 4.5 + 3.6 hours per week (up to 17 hours back per recruiter). Firms automating search/screening are reported as ~90% more likely to staff candidates within 20 days, and full-cycle automation users more than twice as likely to grow revenue. Vendor-conducted, self-reported and correlational.

2024 Building Service Contractor benchmarking survey (Aspire-sponsored): only 2% of BSCs describe themselves as having fully embraced AI, 6% partially integrated, 27% early exploration, 40% not using; 15% already use autonomous/robotic cleaning equipment (30% considering). Shows commercial cleaning is at an early-digitisation stage, so agent ROI there is mostly office-side (bids, work orders, supply and labor scheduling). Sample size not disclosed on the article page.

Counter-evidence for hiring use cases: an audit of LLM resume retrieval across 500+ resumes and 500+ job descriptions found name-associated favouritism (White-associated names favoured in 85.1% of cases, female-associated names in 11.1%), implying automated screening needs bias auditing and human review. Preprint (arXiv, 2024), not a field experiment.

common_tools: Applicant tracking system / staffing CRM (e.g., Bullhorn - the ATS ecosystem behind Bullhorn's GRID survey of 1,500+ recruitment firms)
Job boards, sourcing databases and boolean/keyword search tools (O*NET 13-1071 sourcing task explicitly covers internet recruiting resources, media ads, job fairs and referrals)
HRIS and payroll platforms for time capture, pay statements and multi-client assignment records
Email and spreadsheets as the default workflow layer - O*NET work context for civil engineers shows 100% use email every day and 76% process/analyse information daily

Accounting / job-costing ERP: ledger and billing systems for service firms (the ACEC AI report was produced with BST Global, an AEC-focused ERP vendor, indicating ERP-centric data estates in engineering firms)
Cleaning operations and field-service software (e.g., Aspire, sponsor of the 2024 BSC benchmarking survey) plus timekeeping for dispersed crews, IoT/smart-building and cleaning-validation tech
CAD/BIM and code-compliance tooling (AutoCAD/Revit-class; Autodesk contributed to the ACEC AI report)
Proposal/RFP production: Word/PDF templates, document management, e-signature, CRM opportunity records
constraints: New Jersey Temporary Workers' Bill of Rights (fully effective 5 Aug 2023): staffing firms must issue a written assignment notification statement at dispatch, in English and the worker's primary language, covering worksite, client, wages, transportation, clothing/training and sick-leave rights; 48-hour notice of schedule/shift/location changes; pay parity with the client's comparable employees; itemised pay statements; six-year record retention. Any agent touching placement paperwork must generate accurate, auditable documents - this is both the biggest automation opportunity and the biggest compliance risk in NJ staffing.

PII and background-check sensitivity in staffing: NJ rules forbid charging temporary workers for criminal background checks, consumer reports or drug tests, and pay/assignment data is individually identifiable. Candidate SSNs, I-9 documents and client worksite data call for private or on-prem processing and strict access control.

Algorithmic screening bias risk: LLM resume retrieval has been shown to favour name-associated demographics (preprint, arXiv 2407.20371), so screening agents need documentation, bias testing and human decision-making to survive EEO scrutiny.

Professional engineering accountability: AI cannot replace the judgement of a licensed Professional Engineer and output must be reviewed and sealed by the responsible licensee (NCEES model rules; state board guidance such as North Carolina's July 2025 AI guidelines). Agents can draft proposals and check compliance but cannot sign.

Client confidentiality and NDAs dominate consultancies and agencies; losing confidential bid, pricing or client data to a third-party model is a contract and reputational event, favouring private deployments and retrieval restricted to client-scoped repositories.

Healthcare/pharma staffing (Middlesex County's largest employing sector is Health Care and Social Assistance) adds HIPAA exposure whenever agents touch patient-adjacent scheduling or credentialing data.

Commercial cleaning is physical and safety-regulated: chemical handling procedures and site-safety monitoring (O*NET 37-2011 importance 79-80) mean agents can advise on work orders but not substitute for on-site labour or safety judgement.
trends: Softer NJ labour market: the state's benchmarked 2025 annual unemployment rate was 5.2%, up from 4.6% in 2024 (US 4.3% in 2025), which reduces hiring urgency for staffing clients and squeezes placement margins.
NJ Professional and Business Services employment was 706.5 thousand in Feb 2026, down 0.9% year over year - the sector that buys consulting, staffing and agency services is contracting, not growing.

Middlesex County covered employment was 431,798 in Sept 2025 (+0.3% year over year) and 441,107 in Dec 2025 (+0.4%), with average weekly wages of $1,567 (Q3 2025) and $1,692 (Q4 2025) - a high-wage, slow-growth local base.

Commercial cleaning: recruiting/retaining staff has been the top business challenge for at least three straight years (50% cite it as a challenge to a large extent in 2024, vs 47% in 2023 and 57% in 2022), followed by maintaining profitable margins (39%) and winning new bids/contracts (36%) - i.e., the pressure points are labour, price and bid throughput.

Cleaning labour churn: trade and vendor surveys report annual frontline turnover around 200%, with ranges from 75% to 400% cited across sources - each churn cycle re-creates onboarding, assignment-notification and payroll paperwork.

Engineering consultancies expect AI to absorb volume rather than headcount: 85% of firms see AI as essential to success and 74% expect to maintain staffing while increasing output (ACEC Research Institute, 2025), with marketing/sales and proposals as the leading use case.

Staffing sector AI adoption is broad but shallow: 67% of surveyed firms had bought, built or were experimenting with AI (Bullhorn GRID 2025), while cleaning remains at 2% 'fully embraced' AI (BSC 2024) - an adoption gap that favours a services partner selling done-for-you agents.

Inference (not directly stated in a source): demand in these segments is calendar-driven - commercial cleaning and janitorial staffing track office/school facility schedules, staffing volumes spike with client fiscal-year hiring, and agency/proposal work clusters around public bid cycles - so agent capacity should be planned for seasonal peaks rather than flat load.
caveats: Wage figures are BLS OEWS May 2025 as republished by O*NET for New Jersey statewide and the New York-Newark-Jersey City metro area (Middlesex County's metro); OEWS metro-division figures for Edison-New Brunswick specifically were not retrievable because BLS OEWS data pages redirected and the OEWS API series IDs did not resolve, so county-level medians should be treated as approximations of the metro figure. O*NET task importance scores measure how important a task is to the occupation, not how automatable it is. The strongest measured productivity evidence (QJE 2025, Science 2023, Organization Science 2025) comes from large-firm call centres, simulated professional writing and BCG consulting tasks - not from NJ staffing agencies, engineering consultancies or cleaning contractors, so effect sizes should be presented as transfers with the setting named. The industry-level percentages from ACEC and the BSC benchmarking survey are self-reported expectations from association surveys (and the BSC survey is vendor-sponsored), not measured time savings. The staffing ROI numbers (14.6 hours/week searching, up to 17 hours returned) are vendor research from Bullhorn and correlational. The turnover range (75-400%) comes from trade and vendor sources with inconsistent definitions. No peer-reviewed measurement of AI savings in RFP/bid production or janitorial scheduling was found. Two accuracy flags: the BJ/arXiv bias study and the French employment-service chatbot study are working papers/preprints cited with that limitation noted in the finding text.
data_gaps: No NJ-specific or Middlesex County-specific measurement of AI time savings in staffing, engineering consulting, marketing agencies or commercial cleaning was found; all measured effect sizes come from other geographies and larger firms.

OEWS metro-division detail for Edison-New Brunswick, NJ (Middlesex County) could not be opened; BLS /oes/ data pages redirected to the tables index and the OEWS public API returned 'series does not exist' for attempted series. Wage figures used are NJ statewide plus NY-Newark-Jersey City metro.

Employment counts and wages for segment-specific roles (agency account managers, recruiters by vertical, cleaning account managers, proposal coordinators) are not published separately and had to be proxied by broader SOC codes.

No credible measured estimate of time saved per RFP/bid response, per janitorial work order, or per invoice/AP cycle in these segments was located; vendor case studies exist but were excluded as marketing.
The 2024 BSC benchmarking survey article does not disclose sample size, so its percentages cannot be weighted by firm size.
Peer-reviewed evidence on agentic (multi-step, tool-using) systems in back-office service workflows is essentially absent; current evidence covers assistive copilots on single tasks.
No data retrieved on NJ-specific AI regulation affecting hiring (e.g., pending state bills) beyond the Temporary Workers' Bill of Rights; that area may change and should be re-checked.
